y10-0: Intravenous or gas anaesthesia for major surgery: no difference in recovery
y10-1: In the VITAL trial, led by the University of Warwick and the Royal Marsden Hospital in England and published in JAMA, 2,507 patients aged 50 and over having major planned non-cardiac surgery at 49 NHS hospitals were randomly divided into two groups: one group received anaesthesia through a continuous intravenous infusion of propofol (total intravenous anaesthesia), the other through inhaled gases such as sevoflurane. There was no meaningful difference in the number of days alive and out of hospital in the 30 days after surgery. Major complications, delirium and death were also similar at 30 days, 90 days and 6 months. Patients given intravenous anaesthesia reported less thirst, hoarseness, nausea and vomiting the day after surgery; costs and quality of life over six months were also similar.
y10-2: The trial was not blinded: patients knew which method they had received, which may have affected outcomes they reported themselves, such as nausea. All patients were treated in England, so the results may not transfer directly to other health systems. Long-term cancer outcomes and environmental impact were not examined. As there was no meaningful difference in recovery between the two methods, the choice can be made together with your anaesthetist.
y10-3: Sources: University of Warwick, October 2026 · JAMA, 13 October 2026
y10-4: Three brain pathways linked to depression relief with deep brain stimulation
y10-5: In a study published in the American Journal of Psychiatry, researchers at Mount Sinai in the US examined data, pooled from several separate groups, on patients with severe treatment-resistant depression who had deep brain stimulation (DBS) electrodes implanted in the subcallosal cingulate region of the brain. The researchers modelled the electrical field created by the electrodes on computer and combined it with brain connectivity maps. Lasting improvement was consistently linked to stimulation reaching three white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, the forceps minor, and the medial uncinate fasciculus with the ventral amygdalofugal pathway. In patients who had not responded after two years, the stimulation was not reaching the left cingulum bundle.
y10-6: This study looked at data from existing groups of patients together; whether placing electrodes to target these pathways improves outcomes has not yet been tested. Not every patient had their own brain scan; the press release did not give the number of patients or response rates. Some of the authors are consultants to the device company to which the method is licensed. DBS is a surgical method used only for severe depression that has not responded to other treatments.
y10-7: Sources: ScienceDaily (Mount Sinai), 18 October 2026 · American Journal of Psychiatry, 1 October 2026
y10-8: Structured exercise during cancer treatment: longer survival, fewer recurrences
y10-9: A systematic review and meta-analysis published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine brought together 21 randomised trials of structured exercise programmes in people with cancer: 8,449 participants (88% women, average age 54, average follow-up 64 months), most often with breast cancer, followed by bowel and pancreatic cancer. In those who took part in an exercise programme, the likelihood of death in the overall survival analysis was 23% lower, the likelihood of recurrence before death 17% lower and cancer-specific death 26% lower. Aerobic exercise alone or combined with strength training was linked to better survival; the evidence for strength training alone rested on a single small trial. The association was stronger in those who completed at least 70% of their programme, and the benefit was greatest in early-stage disease.
y10-10: There was no clear evidence that exercise delayed the progression of cancer. People in the comparison groups may also have adopted healthier habits; the type, duration and intensity of exercise varied widely between trials, and most of the evidence comes from breast cancer, with little data on advanced disease. Talk to your treatment team before starting to exercise.
y10-11: Sources: BMJ Group, 15 September 2026 · British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2026
